questions.prompt: A bucket policy allows `s3:GetObject` to `Principal: "*"` with the condition `StringLike` on `aws:SourceVpc` = `vpc-*`. Is the bucket public?
choices: Yes: S3 treats a wildcard-principal statement as public unless a condition pins it to fixed values; anyone can send requests through a VPC endpoint in their own account, and every VPC ID matches vpc-*
No: requests from the internet carry no aws:SourceVpc and are refused, and that is all public means
No: the condition limits access to requests that come from a VPC
Only if the bucket also has an ACL that grants AllUsers
questions.explanation: S3 assumes a policy is public and clears it only when the statement is pinned by fixed values (no wildcards or policy variables) of keys such as aws:SourceVpc, aws:SourceVpce or aws:PrincipalOrgID. The AWS documentation uses this exact vpc-* policy as an example of a public one.

questions.prompt: A bucket's ACL grants READ to the AllUsers group. The bucket has no Block Public Access configuration, and the account-level settings are all four true. What should a posture scanner report?
choices: A critical public bucket, because the bucket itself has no Block Public Access configuration
The public ACL at low severity, marked neutralised: IgnorePublicAcls at the account level makes S3 ignore it, and turning that setting off would make the bucket public again
Nothing: the account-level settings make the ACL irrelevant for good, so there is nothing to record
A gap, because the bucket and account settings conflict and the effective value is unknown
questions.explanation: S3 enforces the most restrictive combination of bucket, account and organization settings, so the effective IgnorePublicAcls is true. The grant is still stored on the bucket; block public access does not modify ACLs, so the finding stays, at low severity, until the ACL itself is fixed.

questions.prompt: A network ACL has inbound rule 90 deny tcp 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 and rule 100 allow tcp 0-65535 from 0.0.0.0/0. Which admin ports can the internet reach through it?
choices: Neither 22 nor 3389, because a deny for the whole internet exists
Both, because rule 100 allows every port and allows take precedence in a network ACL
Only 22, because the higher rule number is evaluated first
Only 3389: rules are evaluated in rule-number order and the first match wins, so 22 hits the deny at 90 and 3389 falls through to the allow at 100
questions.explanation: Network ACLs are stateless and ordered: the lowest-numbered matching rule decides. A posture check that only asks whether an allow exists reports 22 wrongly; one that ignores port ranges misses 3389. posture walks the rules in order for each port.

questions.prompt: A scan shows no security group findings, and its gaps list contains `ec2 describe-security-groups: UnauthorizedOperation`. What do you conclude about the security groups?
choices: They are fine: no findings means no group is open to the internet
The account has no security groups in this Region
Nothing: the scanner could not read them, so those checks did not run; give the collecting role read access (for example SecurityAudit) and collect again
They are fine, but the instances that use them are not
questions.explanation: An error that means 'not configured' (NoSuchBucketPolicy) is data; an error that means 'could not look' (AccessDenied, UnauthorizedOperation) is a gap. Reporting gaps separately is what stops a scanner with missing permissions from printing a clean account.

questions.prompt: Checkov passes the Terraform for an account's trail and IAM users, yet posture reports cloudtrail-no-multi-region and user-key-old on the running account. Which explanation fits?
choices: Both are runtime facts: whether a trail IsLogging and how old an access key is exist only in the running account, which a scan of source code cannot see
posture reads the Terraform state file and Checkov reads the source, so they disagree
The two tools use different CIS benchmark numbering, so the same finding looks different
Checkov is misconfigured, because both tools read the same data
questions.explanation: Static scanners evaluate what the code declares before deploy; posture scanners evaluate what the APIs report after. A multi-Region trail that was created but never started, keys made outside Terraform, console changes and root MFA are invisible to the first and visible to the second.

questions.prompt: An audit report says an account 'fails CIS 1.4' because the root user has no MFA. Why is that statement incomplete, and what makes it unambiguous?
choices: It needs the AWS Region, because CIS sections are numbered per Region
It is complete, because CIS section numbers never change between versions
CIS numbers move between versions (root MFA is 1.5 in v3.0.0 and 1.4 in v5.0.0), so name the benchmark version and add the stable Security Hub control ID, IAM.9
It needs the Checkov check ID, because Checkov defines the CIS sections
questions.explanation: CIS v5.0.0 removed a section 1 recommendation, renumbering everything after it; EBS default encryption moved from 2.2.1 to 5.1.1. Security Hub control IDs map to several standards and versions and stay fixed, so a finding should carry both.
